content: H1N2 is a subtype of the Influenza A virus, which is sometimes referred to as the bird flu virus. This virus is currently endemic in both human and pig populations. Among humans, the only known Influenza A virus subtypes currently circulating are H1N1, H1N2, and H3N2. The emergence of the new A(H1N2) strain is believed to have resulted from the reassortment of genetic material between the circulating Influenza A(H1N1) and A(H3N2) subtypes. The hemagglutinin (HA) protein of the A(H1N2) virus is similar to that of the currently circulating A(H1N1) viruses, while its neuraminidase (NA) protein resembles that of the A(H3N2) viruses. The origin of the A(H1N2) virus remains unknown. However, on February 6, 2002, the World Health Organization (WHO) in Geneva and the Public Health Laboratory Service (PHLS) in the United Kingdom reported the identification of the Influenza A(H1N2) virus in human cases from England, Israel, and Egypt. Additionally, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) identified the A(H1N2) virus in patient specimens collected during the 2001–2002 and 2002–2003 influenza seasons. Historically, Influenza A(H1N2) viruses have circulated transiently. For example, between December 1988 and March 1989, 19 isolates of the A(H1N2) virus were identified in six cities in China, but the virus did not spread further. The H1N2 virus is not significantly different from the currently circulating influenza viruses. Its H1 protein is similar to that of the H1N1 viruses, and its N2 protein is comparable to that of the H3N2 viruses. However, it is uncommon to see the H1 and N2 proteins combined on the same virus. Importantly, the A(H1N2) virus does not appear to cause more severe illness than other influenza viruses, and no unusual increases in influenza activity have been associated with this strain. Because the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase proteins of the A(H1N2) virus closely match those of viruses included in the current influenza vaccine, the vaccine is expected to provide effective protection against A(H1N2). It also offers protection against the currently circulating A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B viruses.
